captions.instagram:
How does a jellyfish swim?

A jellyfish has one ring of muscle, no brain and no bones, yet it is one of the thriftiest swimmers ever measured. Watch its bell squeeze, spring back and ride a ring of its own swirling water.

→ A moon jellyfish has no brain, no bones and no heart, and is about 96% water.
→ Each stinging cell fires a barbed thread in about 700 billionths of a second.
→ One ring of muscle squeezes the bell, and the springy jelly pops it open again.
→ As the bell refills, a second swirl under it gives a moon jelly a free push.
→ Tall jellies jet: faster, but a narrow, fast jet costs far more energy.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/jellyfishclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a jellyfish swim? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A jellyfish has one ring of muscle, no brain and no bones, yet it is one of the thriftiest swimmers ever measured. Watch its bell squeeze, spring back and ride a ring of its own swirling water.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/jellyfishclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/jellyfishclear

In this video:
• A bell of jelly. A moon jellyfish is about 96% water.
• Squeeze, spring back, glide. The muscle squeezes the bell and pushes water out; the springy jelly pops it open again for free.
• Drifting, balancing, steering. Jellies swim a few centimetres a second, so currents carry them: they are plankton.
• From polyp to jellyfish. A larva settles on a rock and becomes a polyp that clones itself, then splits into a stack of discs that pop off as eight-armed baby jellies.
• Blooms, stings and dinner. CMFRI has counted swarms of up to 800 jellies in one net off Kerala, and swarms have shut the Kalpakkam power plant's cooling water.
• How we found out. Romanes cut the rim off a jelly in the 1870s and the bell stopped.
